title: Predictors of Early Mortality After Open Aorto-Iliac Reconstruction in Patients with Aortoiliac Occlusive Disease: An Observational Cohort Study
authors: Merei Imanbayev; Altay Dyussupov; Bekzhigit Tussupkanov; Ergali Muratzhanov; Ardak Mautbekova; Dinara Kozubayeva; Rustam Mukhametkhanov; Rail Gafurov; Nurbek Irgebayev; Dainius Pavalkis; Evgeniy Zhuravlev; Yersyn Sabitov
abstract: Background and Objectives: Open aorto-iliac reconstruction (AIR) for aorto-iliac occlusive disease (AIOD) remains a high-risk procedure due to multifocal atherosclerosis affecting coronary, cerebrovascular, and renal arterial beds. This study aimed to identify factors independently associated with 30-day mortality and explore factors associated with late mortality during available follow-up among 30-day survivors following open AIR. Materials and Methods: An observational, non-randomised cohort of 170 consecutive patients undergoing open AIR for AIOD between January 2018 and December 2024 was analysed. Univariate logistic regression was performed for 30-day mortality; given the limited number of events (n = 16), the primary multivariable analysis used penalized likelihood logistic regression (Firth correction). Late survival among 30-day survivors (landmark cohort, n = 154) was analysed using Kaplan–Meier methods and exploratory univariate Cox proportional hazards regression, with surviving patients censored at the last available follow-up; multivariable Cox modelling was not performed due to the limited number of late events (n = 10). Results: Thirty-day mortality was 9.4% (16/170) in the overall cohort. In the primary Firth penalized multivariable logistic regression, factors associated with 30-day mortality were: severe left IIA stenosis ≥ 70% (OR 9.68; 95% CI 3.08–30.43; p = 0.0001), chronic kidney disease (OR 3.62; 95% CI 1.03–12.66; p = 0.044), and increasing aortic cross-clamp duration, analysed continuously (OR 1.022 per minute; 95% CI 1.000–1.045); a conventional ≥60 min categorical threshold showed a consistent secondary association (OR 4.15; 95% CI 1.28–13.46; p = 0.018). Non-inclusion of IIA was associated with increased 30-day mortality on univariate analysis (OR 4.80; 95% CI 1.31–17.62; p = 0.018). Among the 154 patients entering the 30-day landmark cohort, 10 late deaths were observed during available follow-up. In exploratory univariate Cox regression, intraoperative blood loss was the only statistically significant factor associated with late mortality (HR 1.07 per 100 mL; 95% CI 1.03–1.12; p = 0.0006). Conclusions: Severe IIA disease, chronic kidney disease, and increasing aortic cross-clamp duration (analysed continuously) were independently associated with increased 30-day mortality after open AIR. Intraoperative blood loss was associated with late mortality in exploratory univariate survival analysis. These findings require validation in larger prospective cohorts with longer and more uniform follow-up.

title: Early applications of apple vision pro in clinical medicine and medical education: a scoping review
authors: Yiwei Hu; Yaqin Wang; Xiaohua Zuo; Haibo Hu; Bo Min; Chengxiang Wang; Chengxiang Wang; Zilong Tang; Ning Xiao; Chenjun Huang; 王储蓄; 王储蓄
abstract: The Apple Vision Pro (AVP), a next-generation spatial computing device, has demonstrated potential applications in multidisciplinary clinical diagnosis, treatment, and medical education, by leveraging its unique technical architecture and performance advantages. In clinical practice, its fundamental advantages of three-dimensional (3D) visualization, real-time image integration, and immersive interaction have been preliminarily employed in disease diagnosis and treatment, surgical planning, precise operations, and postoperative rehabilitation across multiple disciplines. In medical education, AVP surpasses the limitations of conventional models, offering a novel methodology for anatomy education, clinical skills development, specialized practical training, and collaboration of distance learning, thereby alleviating persistent challenges such as unequal distribution of teaching resources, low efficiency in skills and specialized training, and the high cost of distance education. However, AVP faces some limitations, including limited hardware portability, insufficient system compatibility, a lack of specialized medical applications, high costs, and incomplete medical certification. Currently, most evidence derives from feasibility studies, case reports, and opinion pieces. Only two Stage 2b confirmatory studies were identified. Thus, high-level evidence for clinical benefit remains scarce. Readers should interpret all reported benefits as preliminary technical demonstrations rather than established clinical outcomes. Future advancements necessitate iterative development of lightweight hardware design, development of specialized medical software, cross-system optimization, and establishment of standardization protocols. Moreover, more randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and multicenter studies are urgently needed to fully explore and validate its intrinsic value in precision medicine and the equitable allocation of medical resources.

title: Pediatric Venous Excess Ultrasound Score (P-VExUS): a novel approach to assess central venous pressure in the PICU
authors: Fernando de Lima Carioca; Nayara Hillebrand Franzon; Lívia da Silva Krzesinski; Isabel de Siqueira Ferraz; Roberto José Negrão Nogueira; Tiago Henrique de Souza
abstract: Accurate assessment of central venous pressure (CVP) in critically ill children is important for guiding fluid management but remains challenging, as invasive monitoring is not always feasible and noninvasive tools are limited. We aimed to develop and validate pediatric adaptations of the Venous Excess Ultrasound Score (P-VExUS) for bedside estimation of CVP in mechanically ventilated children. This prospective observational study was conducted in a tertiary-care PICU. Fifty-six mechanically ventilated children were included. Venous Doppler ultrasonography of the inferior vena cava, hepatic, portal, and intrarenal veins was performed at the bedside. Two P-VExUS models were evaluated: (1) a categorical grading system (0-III) and (2) a semiquantitative point-based score (0-7). Diagnostic performance was assessed for predefined, clinically relevant CVP thresholds reflecting low (< 7 mmHg) and elevated (> 12 mmHg) venous pressure states using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Both models were significantly associated with measured CVP. For predicting elevated CVP, model 1 showed an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.74 (95% CI 0.61-0.85), with 45% sensitivity and 98% specificity. Model 2 demonstrated superior accuracy (AUROC 0.94, 95% CI 0.84-0.98), with 82% sensitivity and 91% specificity (p < 0.001). For detecting low CVP, model 2 also outperformed model 1 (AUROC 0.80 vs. 0.69; p = 0.02). Intrarenal vein patterns had the highest discriminative ability (AUROC 0.92). CONCLUSION: Pediatric-specific P-VExUS models were feasible and accurate for estimating CVP in critically ill children. The point-based model showed superior diagnostic performance and may represent a promising noninvasive bedside tool for assessing venous congestion. WHAT IS KNOWN: • Elevated central venous pressure (CVP) is associated with adverse outcomes in critically ill children, including mortality and renal dysfunction. • Inferior vena cava-based ultrasound indices have limited accuracy for estimating CVP in mechanically ventilated children, while pediatric adaptations of the Venous Excess Ultrasound Score (VExUS) remain poorly defined. WHAT IS NEW: • This study proposes and evaluates two pediatric adaptations of VExUS, demonstrating superior diagnostic performance of a point-based model for identifying elevated (12 mmHg) and low (7 mmHg) CVP. • Intrarenal venous Doppler showed the highest individual discriminative performance, suggesting potential simplification of venous congestion assessment in critically ill children.

title: Restoration of PINK1/Parkin-associated mitophagy via the NAD+/SIRT1 axis attenuates Kawasaki disease vasculitis
authors: Yifei Qin; Urna Kansakar; Shivangi Pande; Gaetano Santulli
abstract: MITOCHONDRIA, AND THE NAD + /SIRT1 AXIS IN KAWASAKI DISEASEKawasaki disease (KD) is an acute, febrile, systemic vasculitis of unknown etiology that predominantly affects infants and young children, and it remains the leading cause of acquired heart disease in pediatric populations worldwide [1][2][3] .Approximately one quarter of untreated children develop coronary arteritis and/or coronary artery aneurysms, a figure that standard high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin G (IVIG) therapy reduces to roughly 3 to 5 percent.Yet up to 20 percent of patients are IVIGresistant, and these children carry a substantially elevated risk of coronary artery lesions, with a pooled odds ratio of approximately 3.9 compared with IVIGresponsive patients in a recent meta-analysis [4][5][6] .The clinical imperative to find adjunctive or alternative therapies is therefore acute, particularly because IVIG is expensive, of limited availability in low-resource settings, and incompletely protective in a meaningful minority of recipients [7] .

title: Coronary Artery Disease among Patients Undergoing Valve Replacement Surgery: A Retrospective Study of Angiographic Profiles and Predictors at a Southern Indian Tertiary Care Centre
authors: Gailin Bronson Sebastian; Yokesh Madhavan; Venkatesh Babu; Kiron Sukulal; Jai Arthe; Arya Rajesh; Shreya Gailin; Krishna Viju
journal: JOURNAL OF CLINICAL AND DIAGNOSTIC RESEARCH
abstract: Introduction: Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) frequently co-exists with Valvular Heart Disease (VHD). In developing countries like India, the shifting epidemiology from rheumatic to degenerative VHD alters this association. Concomitant CAD drastically dictates surgical strategies, yet local angiographic profile data remains scarce. Aim: To determine the angiographic profile and clinical predictors of CAD in patients undergoing Coronary Angiography (CAG) prior to valve replacement surgery at an Indian tertiary care centre. Materials and Methods: The present retrospective study was conducted at Sree Mookambika Institute of Medical Sciences, Kanyakumari, Tamil Nadu, South India, and analysed data of 200 consecutive patients undergoing preoperative CAG before valve replacement surgery. Demographic profiles, cardiovascular risk factors, echocardiographic parameters, and angiographic findings were reviewed. Patients were stratified into CAD and non CAD cohorts. Obstructive CAD was defined angiographically. Statistical analysis utilised Chi-square and Student’s t-tests. Results: The cohort’s mean age was 55.6±9.3 years; 127 (63.5%) were males (63.5%). Prevalences of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, and tobacco use were 71 (35.5%), 64 (32%), 30 (15%), and 15 (7.5%), respectively. Patients with CAD were significantly older (mean age: 59.2±8.5 vs 53.8±9.1 years; p<0.001) and predominantly males (72 (73.5%) vs. 55 (53.9%); p=0.005). Increasing age and diabetes mellitus emerged as independent predictors of CAD in multivariate analysis (OR 1.09, 95% CI 1.05-1.13; p<0.001 and OR 2.49, 95% CI 1.10-5.63; p=0.028, respectively). No statistically significant association was observed between CAD status and valves involved namely, Mitral Valve Disease (MVD), Aortic Valve Disease (AVD) and combined valve disease or valve surgery performed. AVD showed a non significant trend toward higher prevalence in the CAD group (p=0.11). Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery was the most frequently diseased vessel {49 (50%)}. Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF) was marginally lower in the CAD arm (54.2±12.4% vs 57.1±11.3%; p=0.05), while Atrial Fibrillation (AF) lacked statistical correlation (p=0.89). Conclusion: The CAD in Indian valve replacement candidates was independently associated with advanced age, diabetes mellitus, and standard atherosclerotic risk factors. There was no statistically significant association between presence of CAD and the underlying valve pathology, or the type of surgery performed. Preoperative angiographic screening is critical for precise surgical planning, which should be dictated not only by age but by the presence of cardiovascular risk factors.

title: Translational maturity of artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography varies across cardiovascular diseases
authors: Huanhuan Chen; Jingjuan Huang; Xumin Hou
abstract: Electrocardiography is a widely available and low-cost cardiovascular test, and artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) can identify latent electrical phenotypes beyond conventional interpretation. However, high retrospective discrimination does not necessarily translate into clinically reliable or actionable benefit. This critical narrative review evaluates the translational maturity of AI-ECG across arrhythmias, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cardiac amyloidosis. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 2022, through July 10, 2026, with earlier landmark studies added by backward citation tracking. Seventy-seven publications informed the review. Evidence was appraised using five clinically oriented criteria: intended use, reference-standard reliability, external validation and transportability, clinical actionability, and effects on workflow or patient outcomes. AI-ECG has progressed furthest in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction triage and reduced-left-ventricular-ejection-fraction screening, where prospective or randomized studies have demonstrated workflow or diagnostic-yield benefits, whereas acute myocardial infarction rule-out has reached prospective multicenter diagnostic validation. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy screening has also advanced through international validation and prospective implementation. By contrast, occlusion myocardial infarction detection, prediction of occult or future atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long-term heart-failure prediction, and cardiac amyloidosis remain primarily validation-stage or risk-enrichment applications. Across domains, broader adoption is constrained by label quality, calibration, transportability, operating-threshold selection, and limited patient-outcome evidence. AI-ECG is therefore best positioned as clinician-supervised decision support linked to explicit downstream testing and care pathways.

title: PREECLAMPSIA AS A WINDOW INTO FUTURE CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE: PATHOPHYSIOLOGICAL LINKS, LONG-TERM RISK, AND POSTPARTUM PREVENTION
authors: Rodolfo de Oliveira Medeiros; Feres Abrão; Lorrana de Sousa Landim Xavier; Rodrigo Hara Ariosa; Kellen de Pícoli Alexandre; Hellen Cristine Nunes Gonçalves; Laura Rodrigues Albuquerque; Késia Letícia Scombate; Ana Lídia Correia dos Santos; Eduardo Antônio Ferro Faria; Ana Luiza de Souza; Cynthia de Paula Costa Borba; Luisa Magalhães Rodrigues; Thalles Eduardo Silva Santos; Ana Laura Jorge Manzini; Gabriel Francisco Alves; Wanderson Dieikon Xavier Da Silva; André Marciano Neto; Henrique Felipin Da Silva Evangelista
abstract: Preeclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy that affects a substantial proportion of pregnancies and remains a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity. Beyond its immediate obstetric consequences, a growing body of evidence indicates that women with a history of preeclampsia carry a higher long-term risk of chronic hypertension, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, stroke, and cardiovascular death. Shared risk factors, endothelial dysfunction, antiangiogenic imbalance, and vascular and myocardial changes that persist after delivery may explain this association, which allows pregnancy to be interpreted as an early cardiovascular stress test. At the same time, the history of preeclampsia is still inconsistently recorded in clinical practice, and postpartum follow-up is often fragmented between obstetric and primary care. This review aimed to analyze preeclampsia as a window into future cardiovascular disease, considering the pathophysiological links, the magnitude of long-term risk, and the opportunities for postpartum prevention. This is a narrative literature review, guided by a structured question based on the PICo strategy and directed at studies on the cardiovascular trajectory of women with a history of preeclampsia. The evidence shows a roughly twofold increase in the risk of coronary heart disease, a higher risk of heart failure and stroke, and an earlier onset of chronic hypertension, with a gradient according to the severity, timing, and recurrence of the disorder. Much of the excess risk appears to be mediated by conventional risk factors that emerge in the years following delivery, which favors early detection. Postpartum interventions targeting blood pressure have shown promising results, although evidence on hard cardiovascular outcomes is still lacking. It is concluded that preeclampsia should be incorporated into cardiovascular risk assessment, with structured postpartum follow-up and continuity of care throughout the female life course.

title: Anesthesia Management in Pregnant Women with Cardiac Disease: A Narrative Review
authors: Berrin Günaydın; Nuray Camgöz Eryılmaz; Gözde İnan
abstract: This review addresses the perspective of an obstetric anesthesiologist, focusing on the practical principles of peripartum anesthetic management by integrating current evidence with contemporary guideline recommendations rather than providing a comprehensive overview of cardiovascular disease during pregnancy. It also provides a clinically oriented approach to hemodynamic optimization, delivery planning, neuraxial and general anesthetic management, and the treatment of obstetric cardiac emergencies. Ultimately, this review aims to answer the question every anesthesiologist faces in daily practice: “What should the anaesthesiologist do for cardiac pregnant patient?” Cite this article as: Gunaydin DB, Camgoz Eryilmaz N, Inan G. Anesthesia management in pregnant women with cardiac disease: a narrative review. Eurasian J Med. 2026, 58(4), 1693, doi: 10.5152/eurasianjmed.2026.261693.

title: Inflammatory Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm of Probable Autoimmune Etiology: A Case Report and Literature Review
authors: Alina Pietryszyn-Bilińska 1*; Alicja Podolska 2; Magdalena Moś 2; Aleksandra Kawczyk-Krupka 1
journal: International Journal of Clinical Case Reports and Reviews
abstract: Background: Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm (IAAA) is characterised by a thickened aortic wall and periaortic fibrosis. A subset of cases may be associated with IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD). We describe diagnostic and management challenges in a patient with IAAA and suspected IgG4-RD. Case presentation: A 62-year-old patient with a history of smoking and contrast-induced nephropathy underwent ultrasonography, computed tomography angiography and laboratory testing, including inflammatory markers and immunological assays. Clinical findings: The abdominal aorta measured 38 mm in diameter, with extensive periaortic inflammatory tissue and approximately 91% cross-sectional area stenosis of the left renal artery on CT angiography. ESR was 52 mm/h and CRP was 17 mg/L; serum IgG4 was reported as elevated, but its numerical value was unavailable. Blood and urine cultures were negative. IgG4-RD was suspected but not histologically confirmed. Prednisone 20 mg/day and lercanidipine 20 mg/day were initiated; blood pressure subsequently measured 110/80 mmHg. Long-term treatment response was not documented. Conclusions: IgG4-RD should be considered among the possible causes of IAAA with extensive periaortic fibrosis. Elevated serum IgG4 alone does not establish the diagnosis. Multidisciplinary evaluation, careful exclusion of infection and serial imaging are important, particularly when operative treatment is considered high risk.

title: Revascularize first, resect second: off-pump excision of giant SVG pseudoaneurysm
authors: Aadhya Rakesh; Nishant Saran
journal: General Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery Cases
abstract: BACKGROUND: Saphenous vein graft pseudoaneurysm is a rare late complication of coronary artery bypass grafting. Management is particularly challenging when the pseudoaneurysm-bearing graft remains an active source of myocardial perfusion. A 67-year-old man presented 33 years after coronary artery bypass grafting with progressive exertional dyspnea. Echocardiography demonstrated a large mass abutting the right atrium. Computed tomography angiography showed a 10 × 7 × 6 cm partially thrombosed pseudoaneurysm arising from the saphenous vein graft to the right posterior descending artery, with right atrial compression. Coronary angiography demonstrated pseudoaneurysm filling from the graft, chronic native right coronary artery occlusion, patent mammary grafts, and severe proximal graft stenosis. The heart team considered transcatheter exclusion unsuitable because of the distal entry site, calcific graft disease, and ongoing distal right coronary dependence. Redo off-pump saphenous vein grafting to the right posterior descending artery was performed before old-graft ligation. After transit-time flow measurement confirmed new-graft function, the pseudoaneurysm-bearing graft was ligated proximally and distally and excised en bloc. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. Three-month computed tomography angiography demonstrated a patent new graft without residual pseudoaneurysm. DISCUSSION: This case highlights that graft patency and myocardial dependence should be defined before exclusion of a saphenous vein graft pseudoaneurysm. In selected patients, revascularization before graft sacrifice can be performed off pump, avoiding cardiopulmonary bypass while preserving myocardial perfusion.

title: In Vitro Models to Study Fibroelastic Remodeling of the Endocardium in Congenital Heart Disease
authors: Julia Gaal; Cindy Zajac; Sophie C. Doettl; Magnus von Piechowski; Kerstin Saraci; Viktoria Heide-Marie Weixler; Daniel Diaz‐Gil; Pedro J. del Nido; Ingeborg Friehs
abstract: Congenital heart defects (CHD) are characterized by pathological intracardiac blood flow, exposing the endocardium to disturbed shear stress. This contributes to the development of endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE), a restrictive fibrotic remodeling process associated with diastolic dysfunction. Despite the pathomechanistic role of the endocardium in CHD, EFE-derived endocardial endothelial cells (EdEECs) remain largely understudied. No standardized protocol exists for isolating and purifying them from human pediatric tissue. Tissue from N = 15 pediatric patients with (1) hypoplastic left heart syndrome, (2) pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum, and (3) pulmonary vein stenosis was included. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT). EdEECs were isolated from resected EFE tissue using CD144-based magnetic separation. Enrichment of the endocardial phenotype was evaluated by flow cytometry, immunocytochemistry and RT-qPCR. To mimic disease-like conditions, EdEECs were exposed to in vitro shear stress and transforming growth factor beta 1. EFE driven by fibrogenic activation of EECs through EndMT was observed in the left ventricle, right ventricle, and left atrium in patients with different CHDs. Magnetic CD144-based isolation provided a reliable, gentle approach to purify EdEECs from cardiac tissue, achieving > 95% purity while reproducibly preserving endocardial identity at both the protein and gene expression levels. Isolated EdEECs retained their intrinsic, disease-specific predisposition and vulnerability to EndMT under static, and high shear stress. Unlike healthy EECs (HEECs), physiological, low shear stress alone was not sufficient to restore the intrinsic fibrogenic vulnerability of EdEECs. EndMT-mediated EFE was observed across different CHD entities. A reproducible protocol for isolating and purifying EdEECs from EFE tissue preserves their endocardial phenotype and disease-specific characteristics. This provides a disease-mimicking in vitro model to study EdEEC-specific signaling pathways.

title: Sex-Specific Adaptations in Placental Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Function in babies Born with Critical Congenital Heart Disease
authors: Marie Demonceaux; Alban-Elouen Baruteau; Chloé Cloteau; Mathilde Gourdel; Bénédicte Romefort; Nadir Benbrik; Morgane Vincke; Garance Devarenne; Norbert Winer; Véronique Ferchaud‐Roucher
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the leading cause of birth defects; most critical (c)CHD newborns will develop neurodevelopmental disorders. Abnormal placental development may be involved, as genetics explains only 30% of sporadic CHD cases. Growing evidence suggests that placental dysfunction may result in heart and brain defects, as it shares a common early development. We hypothesized that newborns with critical CHD exhibit sex-specific alterations in placental mitochondrial biogenesis and function which may affect the fetal growth trajectory. Term placenta and paired umbilical cord (UC) blood were collected at birth from cCHD (n=16) and matched control (n=20) neonates. Mitochondrial lipid complex (phosphatidic acid (PA), phosphatidylglycerol (PG), cardiolipin (CL)), acylcarnitine metabolites and organic acids were determined in placenta by LC-MS/MS. Gene expressions of enzymes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics and lipid pathway were measured in placenta by RT-qPCR. Placental protein expressions of β-oxidation and OXPHOS were determined by Western Blot. Mitochondrial dynamics were reduced in cCHD placentas, particularly in male infants. Long-chain acylcarnitine (LC-acar) metabolites decreased in female cCHD placentas and increased in males, while they increased in both sexes in UC plasma. Malonate levels increased in cCHD placentas, affecting the TCA cycle. CL de novo synthesis was dysregulated in the cCHD placentas, though CL concentrations were similar in both groups. The cCHD placenta may compensate for cardiac defect in a potential sex-dependent manner, leading to an accumulation of LC-acylcarnitine in the UC plasma. Placental mitochondrial adaptation to metabolic needs may have a cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects.

title: Symbolic transfer entropy reveals enhanced cardiac autonomic influence on cortical activity in infants with congenital heart disease
authors: Wenjuan Luo; HaiTao Liu; Tiejia Jiang; Xiangming Fan; Qiannan Zhang; Shuhao Zhang; Zhigang Gao
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is associated with neurodevelopmental vulnerability, but directional cardiac–cortical statistical dependencies in early childhood remain incompletely characterized. We analyzed simultaneous electrocardiography and electroencephalography recordings during sleep from 14 infants and toddlers with heterogeneous CHD diagnoses and 16 healthy controls. Heart rate variability features, including the low-frequency/high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio, and EEG band-power features were temporally aligned. Bidirectional symbolic transfer entropy based on amplitude-bin quantization was summarized using a net directionality index. Both groups exhibited predominantly positive net directionality indexes, while the CHD group showed higher net cardiac-to-cortical estimates for LF/HF–alpha and LF/HF–beta under permutation-based false discovery rate control. These exploratory group-level differences do not establish a uniform CHD phenotype, altered physiological coupling or individual clinical risk. Interpretation remains limited by patient heterogeneity, acquisition-setting differences and unresolved effects of the underlying feature statistics. Longitudinal studies and methodological validation are required before considering prognostic or intervention applications.

title: Morphological Study of the Tricuspid Valve in Human Embalmed Hearts
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Background: The tricuspid valve, situated between the right atrium and right ventricle, is a vital component of cardiac anatomy whose morphological variability has significant implications for surgical and interventional cardiac procedures.Anatomical knowledge of its three leaflets-anterior, posterior, and septal-is indispensable for effective valve repair, prosthetic valve design, and understanding functional tricuspid regurgitation.Aims & Objectives: To measure and compare the annular circumference, leaflet length, and leaflet height of the anterior, posterior, and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve in human embalmed cadaveric hearts, and to establish normative morphometric data relevant to clinical and surgical practice. Materials and Methods:A descriptive cross-sectional anatomical study was conducted at Father Muller Medical College, Mangalore, Karnataka, on 50 embalmed human cadaveric hearts.Annular circumference, valve diameter, and the length and height of each leaflet were measured using a thread-and-scale method and measuring tape.Descriptive statistics including mean, standard deviation, and range were calculated for all parameters.Results: The annular circumference ranged from 8.9 to 15.3 cm (mean ± SD: 11.84 ± 1.42 cm) and valve diameter from 2.83 to 4.87 cm (mean: 3.75 ± 0.48 cm).The anterior leaflet was consistently the largest with a mean length of 4.82 ± 0.83 cm and height of 2.04 ± 0.23 cm.The septal leaflet showed intermediate dimensions, while the posterior leaflet was the smallest and most variable.Conclusion: Significant morphometric variability exists in the tricuspid valve across cadaveric specimens.The anterior leaflet was the largest in all measured parameters, while the posterior leaflet demonstrated the greatest variability.These findings provide normative data of practical value for cardiac surgeons, interventional cardiologists, and biomedical engineers involved in prosthetic valve design.

title: Does dapagliflozin (Forxiga) affect the progression or improvement of regurgitation in valvular heart disease?
authors: Tripdatabase
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Evidence shows dapagliflozin can significantly improve mitral regurgitation parameters in the short term for patients with functional mitral regurgitation. Its effects on other types of valvular heart disease remain unclear, indicating the need for further research.

title: Remimazolam-based total intravenous anesthesia for prone cervical spine surgery in a patient with previously undiagnosed dilated cardiomyopathy after aborted anesthetic induction: A case report
authors: Jooyong Lee; Sanghi Park
abstract: Unexpected hemodynamic deterioration during anesthesia induction may show previously undiagnosed cardiac dysfunction. Herein, we report a case of successful remimazolam-based total intravenous anesthesia in a patient with newly diagnosed dilated cardiomyopathy (DCMP) who underwent prone cervical spine surgery. A 113-kg man with quadriplegia owing to cervical spinal cord injury underwent emergency cervical decompression and fusion surgery. Severe desaturation and hypotension developed despite FiO₂ 1.0 during the initial anesthetic attempt using etomidate and sevoflurane-remifentanil anesthesia, and surgery was aborted. A subsequent evaluation showed DCMP with severely reduced left ventricular systolic function. Reoperation was performed under total intravenous anesthesia with remimazolam–remifentanil. Although transient desaturation and reduced tidal volume developed after prone positioning, surgery was completed with relatively stable hemodynamics. In conclusion, remimazolam-based total intravenous anesthesia may be useful in selected high-risk patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction.

title: Effects of violet light exposure on aging dogs: a pilot study
authors: Kana MIYAMOTO; Nanami Ono; Shinichiro Kondo; Yukihiro Miwa; Kazuo Tsubota; Makiko Ozawa; Takefumi Kikusui
abstract: Aging in dogs is known to induce various physical and brain alterations similar to dementia in humans. Concurrently with the recent extension of canine life expectancy, these age-related changes have imposed growing burdens on both dogs and their owners, emerging as a significant social issue. However, no curative treatment has yet been established, and the current mainstay of management focuses on improving the quality of life through symptomatic therapies, such as environmental modifications and pharmacotherapy. This study focused on violet light, which has suggested efficacy against such age-related changes. We developed a novel violet light irradiation device and evaluated its efficacy and safety in elderly dogs as a pilot study. An intra-individual comparison using an ABA design was employed with geriatric dogs aged 14 to 16 years housed in a senior dog care facility (two of which discontinued midway). The study design consisted of a one-month violet light exposure phase preceded and followed by two-week non-exposure periods. Physical activity levels were measured using accelerometers and cognitive function was assessed using the DISHAA and CCDR. To evaluate the safety, general physical and ophthalmic examinations were conducted by veterinarians. As a result, no significant overall effect was found on activity levels (Daytime: x 2 = 4.22, p = 0.12; Nighttime: x 2 = 1.58, p = 0.45). Similarly, no significant overall effects were observed for either the DISHAA or the CCDR (DISHAA: x 2 = 1.60, p = 0.45; CCDR: x 2 = 1.56, p = 0.46). However, a trend toward cognitive improvement was observed in six out of seven dogs and an upward trend in activity levels-indicating physical function improvement-was noted in two out of seven dogs. Regarding safety, no overt clinical abnormalities associated with violet light irradiation were identified. This pilot study demonstrated no clear overall effect, though some individuals showed signs of improvement. Future research should consider large-scale trials controlling for various variables.

title: Pre-Anesthetic Venous Excess Ultrasound Score for Predicting Spinal Anesthesia-Induced Hypotension in Geriatric Patients Undergoing Elective Lower Body Surgeries: A Prospective Observational Study
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Background: Spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension (SAIH) complications are still prevalent in 16-33% of cases.Objectives: To assess the correlation between the pre-anesthetic venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) grading system and the prediction of SAIH in elderly patients, as well as the correlation between internal jugular vein (IJV) measurements and SAIH prediction in geriatric patients.Methods: This prospective observational investigation included 127 patients aged ≥ 65 years at Tanta University Hospitals over one year.All patients were divided into two groups: Group A (n = 56) with no SAIH and Group B (n = 71) with SAIH.A comprehensive evaluation of prominent systemic veins, including hepatic, portal, renal, and internal jugular veins, was performed on all patients.Results: Delta IJV diameter (ΔIJV-D), delta IJV area (ΔIJV-A), and IJV collapsibility index (IJV-CI) were significantly predictive of hypotension.ΔIJV-D showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.697 (P<0.001) at a cutoff >0.11, with 77.46% sensitivity, 57.14% specificity, 69.62% positive predictive value (PPV), and 66.67% negative predictive value (NPV).ΔIJV-A had an AUC of 0.635 (P=0.009) at a cutoff >0.17, with 78.87% sensitivity, 55.36% specificity, 69.14% PPV, and 67.39% NPV.IJV-CI demonstrated an AUC of 0.739 (P<0.001) at a cutoff >19, with 80.28% sensitivity, 76.79% specificity, 81.43% PPV, and 75.44%NPV.Conclusions: Predictors of SAIH in geriatric patients include the simplicity and noninvasiveness of pre-anesthetic IJV-CI, ΔIJV-A, and ΔIJV-D.In contrast, VExUS did not predict SAIH during perioperative assessment.

title: Prosthetic Aortic Valve Infective Endocarditis Complicated With Malignant Arrhythmias: Diagnostic and Management Challenges
authors: Imthiaz Manoly; Safia Fathima Anver Pasha; Mohannad  M Al Asaad; Nayyer R Siddiqi
abstract: Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) remains a serious, life-threatening complication of cardiac valve replacement, with outcomes significantly determined by timely recognition, multidisciplinary management, and appropriate surgical intervention.We report the case of a 59-year-old man with a prior mechanical aortic valve replacement, previously treated for iron deficiency anemia with recommended further workup but lost to follow-up, who presented with chest pain, hemodynamic compromise, and cardiac arrhythmias.Echocardiography confirmed severe prosthetic valve dehiscence with a paravalvular leak and peri-aortic root abscess consistent with PVE; blood cultures grew Staphylococcus epidermidis.His course was complicated by cardiogenic shock secondary to severe aortic regurgitation and bradyarrhythmias requiring emergency transvenous pacing.Despite an urgent redo aortic valve replacement with aortic root reconstruction and perioperative veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support, he subsequently developed refractory malignant arrhythmias and could not be resuscitated despite extensive efforts.This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of PVE presenting with nonspecific features, the surgical complexity of valve replacement in the setting of advanced aortic root and periannular destruction, and the catastrophic potential of postoperative malignant arrhythmias following complex infective endocarditis surgery.It underscores the critical importance of early recognition, dedicated endocarditis teams, and the need for further research into the management of postoperative arrhythmias in this high-risk population.

title: The durability of different anchoring points and anchoring types in the left ventricle in an ex vivo porcine model
authors: Henrik Bjursten; Per N Wierup; Sasha M. Koul; Matthias Götberg; Magnus Dencker
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Surgical mitral valve repair, including anchoring in different parts of the mitral apparatus, is the standard of care for severe mitral regurgitation. Various percutaneous approaches have been developed and are currently under development, but are struggling with durable results. This study investigates the durability of different anatomic anchoring points and anchoring types in the left ventricle. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Anchoring was tested with PTFE sutures or a 5 mm helix at three locations: the head of the papillary muscle, the lateral wall of the ventricle, and the apex of the ventricle. An accelerated life test was performed with 300 cycles at 3 N for each anchoring. Durability was assessed by measuring compliance (strain in mm until 3 N is reached), migration (change in strain from the first to the last cycle), and the occurrence of dehiscence. RESULTS: The lowest numerical strain/compliance in the first cycle was observed at the head of the papillary muscle anchoring (both surgical and helix). Migration of strain limits over 300 cycles was seen for all locations. The lowest migration was numerically for helix in the papillary muscle. CONCLUSION: PTFE in the head of the papillary muscle is standard practice in mitral valve repair and was used as a reference in the present study. The anchoring that yielded the most similar results was a helix in the papillary muscle, whereas other anchoring points showed greater compliance and/or migration.

title: Mitral Transcatheter Edge‐to‐Edge Repair at Centers With and Without On‐Site Cardiac Surgery: A Comparative Registry With a Shared Interventional Team
authors: Giulia Marchisio; Elisa Pelloni; Francesco Pisano; Lorenzo Zaccaro; Laura Contu; Maurizio B. Tusa; Nedy Brambilla; Marco Guerrini; Francesco Bedogni; Paolo Scacciatella
abstract: BACKGROUND: Comparative evidence for M-TEER performed at centers with versus without on-site cardiac surgery is lacking. We compared early outcomes at two centers that shared the same interventional operator team but differed in the availability of on-site cardiac surgery. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed prospectively collected registry data from 64 consecutive patients with severe (4+) MR treated at a center without on-site cardiac surgery (no-CCH, n = 21) and a center with on-site cardiac surgery (CCH, n = 43). The same interventional operator team performed every procedure. At the no-CCH center, surgical expertise was provided through a shared Heart Team and a formal emergency transfer pathway. The cohorts were treated in sequential calendar periods. Principal comparative endpoints were MVARC device and procedural success at 30 days. Exploratory non-inferiority analyses used margins of -12.5% and -10%. RESULTS: MVARC technical success was 100% versus 97.7%. Device and procedural success were each 81.0% versus 72.1% (risk difference [RD] +8.9%, 95% CI -14.9 to +27.5; p = 0.547). Freedom from major MVARC serious adverse events was 95.2% versus 95.3%. Twelve of 16 device-success failures involved a mean transmitral gradient ≥ 5 mmHg. Surgical conversion and in-hospital death were 0% in both centers. CONCLUSIONS: In this preliminary same-team comparison, 30-day MVARC device and procedural success rates were 81.0% at the no-CCH center and 72.1% at the CCH center. Confidence intervals were wide and non-inferiority was not established. These findings support prospective evaluation of network-based M-TEER programs with shared interventional expertise and formal surgical backup.

title: Myocardial scar burden independently predicts response to cardiac resynchronization therapy
journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: Objectives: Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) has been shown to improve quality of life and reduce mortality in patients with heart failure.Around 30 -45% are non-responders to CRT.Determinants of response to CRT have been extensively studied.Faithful efforts were exerted to improve selection criteria for CRT beyond standard measures of electrical dyssynchrony.We aimed to assess the predictive value of amount and distribution of myocardial fibrosis to identify responders to CRT compared to conventional measures.Methodology: 58 patients who underwent CRT implantation on the basis of standard indication were studied.All patients had available myocardial imaging (cardiac MRI or nuclear scan) prior to CRT.Images were analyzed for scar quantification and distribution.Multiple variables were studied.Receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to evaluate the ability of Global scar to predict response to CRT.Results: 30 patients of 58 were non-responders to CRT. 27 patients had non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, while 31 patients had ischemic cardiomyopathy.19 patients (70.3%) in the non-ischemic group, and 9 patients (32.2%) in the ischemic group were responders to CRT, with a statistically significant difference, p-value: 0.002.A cutoff threshold of myocardial scar at 22.9% independently predicted response to CRT with a sensitivity of 70% and a specificity of 92.9%.Conclusion: Global myocardial scar burden predicted response to CRT independent of etiology, regional distribution, and measures of electrical dyssynchrony.

title: Transjugular implantation of a leadless pacemaker in a 97-year-old patient with severe kyphosis and tortuous femoral veins: a case report
authors: Minghuan Fu; Xue-Fei Tao; Jie Gao; Yong Shi; Biao Cheng; Wei Zhang; Xiao-Han Chen
abstract: Background Leadless pacemaker systems offer significant benefits for frail older adults by avoiding pocket- and lead-related complications. However, anatomical challenges including severe spinal deformities and significant venous tortuosity can complicate conventional transfemoral or trans-subclavian implantation. Case report A 97-year-old man with severe kyphosis, tortuous femoral veins, and high-grade atrioventricular block was referred for permanent pacing. Supine positioning for subclavian access was not feasible, and the femoral anatomy posed an unacceptably high procedural risk. Following a multidisciplinary assessment and procedural planning, a transjugular approach was selected. Implantation was performed with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position, using adapted fluoroscopic projections and temporary femoral pacing as backup. An Aveir ventricular response leadless pacemaker was successfully delivered via the right internal jugular vein. Final device parameters were satisfactory, with a sensing amplitude of 8.5 mV, a pacing threshold of 0.5 V at 0.4 ms, and an impedance of 510 Ω. No perioperative complications occurred. At follow-up, exertional dyspnea had resolved, and device performance remained stable. Conclusion This case demonstrates that transjugular implantation of a leadless pacemaker can be a safe and feasible alternative for older adults with complex anatomical limitations that contraindicate standard pacing approaches. Careful preprocedural assessment and adaptation of intraoperative techniques are essential for procedural success in high-risk settings.

title: Residual Mitral Regurgitation After Surgical Mitral Valve Repair and Long-Term Recurrence and Reintervention
authors: JM Kong; Mingyang Yu; Jingxin Zhou
abstract: Surgical mitral valve repair is the preferred treatment for degenerative mitral regurgitation (MR) and is also widely performed for MR of other etiologies; however, recurrent MR after repair is not uncommon and is associated with adverse left ventricular remodeling and increased risks of mitral valve reintervention and death. At the completion of repair, a small amount of residual MR is frequently detected on intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography or predischarge transthoracic echocardiography, and whether mild residual MR is acceptable remains clinically controversial. Existing evidence derives largely from single-center studies with limited sample sizes, and the timing of residual MR assessment, grading thresholds, and outcome definitions vary considerably across studies, limiting the generalizability of their conclusions. We therefore plan to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) will be systematically searched for English-language studies of adults undergoing surgical mitral valve repair for MR of any etiology that report residual MR grade and long-term follow-up outcomes. The primary outcomes are recurrent MR (≥ moderate MR during follow-up) and mitral valve reintervention (surgical or transcatheter). In the primary analysis, adjusted hazard ratios will be pooled using random-effects models; unadjusted estimates will be pooled separately as supplementary analyses and will not be combined with adjusted estimates. Pooled estimates will be obtained separately for different residual MR thresholds (≥ mild vs. none/trace; > mild vs. ≤ mild). Subgroup analyses will be performed according to MR etiology (degenerative vs. other or mixed etiologies) and timing of residual MR assessment (intraoperative vs. early postoperative/predischarge vs. not specified), and the association of residual MR with long-term mortality will also be explored. Because death precludes subsequent reintervention, we will record whether included studies accounted for competing risks, and cause-specific and subdistribution hazard ratios will be pooled together in the primary analysis, with the measure type examined as a subgroup factor and a sensitivity analysis restricted to cause-specific hazard ratios. These analyses will be complemented by risk-of-bias assessment, sensitivity analyses (including recurrent MR defined as ≥ moderate-to-severe MR and reintervention restricted to surgical reoperation), and grading of the certainty of evidence. This study is expected to clarify the prognostic value of residual MR, particularly mild residual MR, thereby providing evidence to inform whether surgeons should aim for no or trace residual MR intraoperatively, whether a second pump run for re-repair is warranted, and how high-risk patients should be stratified for postoperative surveillance, as well as offering a reference for standardizing the definition and reporting of residual MR in future studies.

title: Von Willebrand Factor Biomarkers in Prosthetic Valve Dysfunction
authors: Sameed Arshad; Sabir Khan; Muhammad Zahid
abstract: Imaging remains the foundation of prosthetic valve surveillance because it identifies valve morphology, lesion mechanism, and hemodynamic severity. However, acoustic shadowing, eccentric or multiple regurgitant jets, loading conditions, and reader variability can complicate assessment, particularly for paravalvular regurgitation after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. High shear stress unfolds von Willebrand factor (VWF), promotes proteolysis of its high-molecular-weight multimers, and produces a measurable defect in primary hemostasis. Multimer analysis, closure time with adenosine diphosphate (CT-ADP), and the VWF activity-to-antigen ratio therefore provide a biologic signal of abnormal flow rather than an anatomic image. Prospective studies show that VWF abnormalities track residual paravalvular regurgitation during transcatheter aortic valve replacement, occur with dysfunctional prostheses, change after mitral paravalvular-leak repair, and are associated with bleeding. The evidence nevertheless remains observational; most diagnostic cohorts are small and single-center, thresholds lack independent validation, assays are vulnerable to hematologic and preanalytic confounding, and no completed randomized trial has shown that VWF-guided management improves outcomes. VWF testing is best viewed as an investigational adjunct when imaging and the clinical picture are discordant or when prosthetic dysfunction coexists with otherwise unexplained bleeding. It should not replace guideline-directed echocardiography or be used for routine surveillance outside research protocols.

title: Association between preoperative E/e′ and early left ventricular systolic recovery after coronary artery bypass grafting
authors: Jungsuk Choi; Hee Kyung Kim; Joon Kyu Kang
abstract: Background In patients with reduced or mildly reduced ejection fraction, the degree of systolic recovery after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is heterogeneous. We assessed whether routine preoperative transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) indices—particularly E/e′—are associated with early postoperative improvement in left ventricular function. Methods We retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing isolated CABG at a single tertiary center (April 2019 to July 2025). Eligibility required a preoperative left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of <50%. Emergency/salvage operations, 30-day deaths, and patients without an evaluable early postoperative TTE were excluded. The primary outcome was an absolute increase in the LVEF of ≥10 percentage points. Because of the limited number of outcome events, the primary association analysis used a single-predictor logistic regression model with preoperative E/e′. Sensitivity analyses excluded patients with preoperative atrial fibrillation (AF) and modeled postoperative LVEF as a continuous outcome adjusted for baseline LVEF. Results Of 75 otherwise clinically eligible patients, three lacked an evaluable early postoperative TTE, leaving 72 patients for outcome analysis; 17 (23.6%) achieved an LVEF increase of ≥10 percentage points. A higher preoperative E/e′ was associated with early LVEF improvement (OR 1.155 per 1-unit increase; 95% CI 1.04–1.28; p = 0.005; N = 66; 16 events). The apparent AUC was 0.700; after 1,000-resample bootstrap internal validation, the estimated optimism was 0.004 and the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.696 (95% bootstrap CI 0.526–0.885). The association persisted after excluding patients with AF (OR 1.14; 95% CI 1.02–1.27; p = 0.025). In a sensitivity analysis using postoperative LVEF as a continuous outcome, E/e′ remained associated with postoperative LVEF after adjustment for baseline LVEF ( β = 0.31 percentage points per 1-unit increase; 95% CI 0.01–0.61; p = 0.042). Conclusion A higher preoperative E/e′ was associated with early improvement in LV systolic function after CABG among patients with a preoperative LVEF of <50% who survived to undergo early postoperative echocardiographic assessment. Given the small number of events and the single-center retrospective design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require external validation.

title: Antecedents and consequences of Green-tech FDI in emerging markets
authors: Zhuoran Liu
abstract: As environmental pressures intensify, attracting sustainable foreign direct investment (FDI), particularly green-tech FDI, has become a critical pathway for emerging markets to achieve environmental sustainability. However, existing research remains fragmented, offering limited insights into why green-tech FDI enters emerging markets and how it affects regional green innovation. This thesis addresses these gaps by systematically examining both the antecedents and consequences of green-tech FDI through three empirical studies using regional data from China. Study 1 and Study 2 focus on the antecedents of green-tech FDI. Study 1 examines how host-country conditions can attract green-tech FDI, highlighting the role of environmental management information disclosure (EMID) by domestic firms in reducing information gaps and strengthening green market–seeking motives. Study 2 shifts attention to the active decision-making of green-tech FDI, showing that under uncertainty, green-tech foreign investors engage in identity-based bandwagon learning by imitating peers with similar green identities, thereby mitigating investment risks. Study 3 turns to the consequences of green-tech FDI. It demonstrates that, due to the technological complexity of green innovation and limited absorptive capacity in emerging markets, green-tech FDI may generate crowding-out effects rather than purely positive spillovers. Adopting a network perspective, the study further finds that universities play a key moderating role: through broad linkages and deep collaborations, they help mitigate negative spillovers and facilitate the diffusion of green technologies. Together, the three studies advance the literature on sustainable FDI by differentiating green-tech FDI from general FDI and identifying the specific mechanisms that shape its entry decisions and local innovation outcomes. Practically, the findings provide guidance for emerging-market governments and firms on how to attract and manage sustainable investment, balance growth with environmental objectives, and strengthen local innovation ecosystems.

title: Combating Data and Target Shifts in Visual Tasks
authors: Zhaorui Tan
abstract: The rapid advancement of deep learning models for visual tasks has led to significant progress in many domains. However, a key challenge remains: ensuring that models can generalize effectively to unseen samples or novel classes, especially in real-world scenarios where training data-target pairs are often limited or unavailable, and test data may exhibit shifts in both data and targets. This thesis addresses the problem of shifts across data and targets, proposing novel methods to improve model generalization and transferability in complex settings. The thesis identifies the different shift scenarios for visual tasks and presents their problem forms. The research first relaxes the static target distribution assumption in Multi-Domain Generalization (mDG) tasks, introducing the General Multi-Domain Generalization (GMDG) objective to improve generalization under varying data shifts. Specifically, Extensive experiments validate that GMDG is feasible for classification, segmentation, and regression tasks. Further considering extreme target distribution shifts where even unknown novel classes emerge, the study also explores logical regularization techniques for tasks such as Generalized Category Discovery (GCD), mDG+GCD, and Class Incremental Learning (CIL), proposing a sample-based logical regularization term (L-Reg) to enhance data-, target-, and all-shift generalization. Additionally, a partial logic framework is introduced to address challenges in CIL, enabling models to retain room for unknown classes during training. This is further extended by the Partial-Logic Regularization (PL-Reg), which improves generalization across GCD, mDG+GCD, and transferability for CIL tasks. Furthermore, the thesis proposes a novel Semantic-aware Data Augmentation (SADA) framework for cross-modality generalization in text-to-image synthesis (T2Isyn), text-image retrieval (TIR), and image-text retrieval (ITR) tasks. This framework ensures semantic preservation across text and image modalities, improving both semantic consistency and image quality in cross-modality tasks. The methods proposed in this thesis offer significant advancements in visual generalization and transfer scenarios, providing theoretical insights and practical solutions for handling data shifts, target shifts, and multi-modalities in complex scenarios. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, demonstrating their superior performance across a range of tasks.

title: Depth of Processing, learner aptitude, and the acquisition of L2 English grammatical structures
authors: Shweta Nigam
abstract: Depth of Processing (DoP) is central to several models of instructed second language acquisition (ISLA) (Leow, 2015). While DoP has been extensively examined in vocabulary learning (e.g., Laufer & Hulstijn, 2001), its role in the acquisition of grammatical structures, particularly through oral and audio-visual modalities remains comparatively underexplored. Drawing on the Levels of Processing framework (Craik & Lockhart, 1972), this study investigated whether task-induced processing depth influences the acquisition of third conditionals and comparatives, and whether language aptitude (LLAMA B, D, F) predicts learning gains. Using a pretest–posttest design, four intact classes involving 108 Grade 8 EFL learners in India were assigned to one of the three experimental conditions differing in level and type of processing: Low DoP, High DoP Explicit, and High DoP Implicit. The treatment task required the participants to listen to an audio-visual story containing the target structures (third conditionals and comparatives) and complete analytic tasks (varying in different groups) before listening to the story for a second time. The oral performance of the participants was analysed for accuracy, and frequency of use of the target structures. A grammaticality judgement test (GJT) and an elicited imitation task (EIT) were used to assess the participants’ gains in the knowledge of the target structures. In addition, language aptitude (LLAMA B, D, F) was measured and modelled as a predictor of gain scores. Results showed a significant effect of processing condition on GJT performance with the High DoP Implicit group outperforming the High DoP Explicit group on total scores and comparatives. In contrast, ANCOVA analyses indicated no significant group differences on EIT outcomes once pretest performance was controlled, with pretest scores strongly predicting posttest performance. In oral production, processing effects were structure-specific: the Low DoP group showed greater accuracy gains for comparatives, while both High DoP groups revealed increased frequency of use of third conditionals. However, across all four measures, multiple regression analyses indicated that LLAMA B, D, and F did not significantly predict gain scores. Overall, the findings support a processing-by-structure pattern: deeper processing benefits were most evident for the more salient structure (comparatives) on an explicit, written measure, whereas complex, low-salience forms (third conditionals) showed limited accuracy change but increased frequency of use under deeper processing.

title: A UAV-Based Framework for Community-Scale Residential Building Energy Modelling in China
authors: Mengfan Jin
abstract: With increasing emphasis on energy efficiency and carbon emission reduction in the building sector, rapid and scalable energy modelling of existing buildings is critical for retrofit projects and policy development. Conventional surveys, data collection and energy modelling processes remain labour-intensive and impractical for large-scale applications, and energy modelling often dominates project time and cost. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) equipped with high-resolution and infrared cameras now offer fast and safe exterior surveys, showing great potential in building energy assessments. Yet, a systematic framework for UAV integration, from image capture through processing to inputs for building energy simulation, has not been established. This research addresses these challenges by developing a structured framework for community-scale building energy modelling, which integrates UAV photogrammetry to accelerate data acquisition, reduce labour, and shorten energy modelling time for retrofit projects. The framework is designed to minimise prior data requirements while maximising automation and retaining sufficient accuracy and reliability. It also addressed systemic issues, such as the lack of data necessary to fully exploit the potential of available technologies in the context of this study. To achieve this research objective, a mixed-methodology approach, combining desk studies and fieldwork, was adopted. First, a comprehensive review of UAV-based building energy studies mapped the current applications and available tools, proposing a preliminary framework. Fieldwork then encompassed a pilot study and a detailed case study. In the pilot test, a single building was surveyed to identify an optimal toolchain for flight planning, image capture, photogrammetric reconstruction, model generation, and selection of a simulation platform. The resulting refined framework was applied to a case study of a 39-building community, and it was demonstrated that further automation was necessary. The potential for automation was then further explored. Geomatic algorithms, machine learning, and deep learning techniques were compared, and the combination that best balanced accuracy and processing time was selected for 3D model generation and window-to-wall ratio (WWR) extraction. In parallel, an archetype library of residential buildings in the Hot Summer Cold Winter (HSCW) zone in China was compiled to facilitate the assignment of thermal parameters. Finally, a reusable community-scale building energy modelling (CBEM) workflow was assembled in Grasshopper using Ladybug Tools components to process the aforementioned inputs. In conclusion, this study integrates UAV photogrammetry, GIS-based geomatic algorithms, machine learning, and graphical programming to develop an UAV-CBEM framework. The outcomes establish a foundation for scalable UAV-based building energy assessments, enhancing applicability in data-limited and large-scale settings worldwide.

title: Spectral Materialism: Encounters with land-time-scapes
authors: Nightingale, Sam
abstract: This transdisciplinary, practice-based PhD introduces spectral materialism through art-based research encounters with ecologically and historically stratified land-time-scapes shaped by hypersalinity and colonial terraforming. Centred in the semi-arid Mallee (southeastern Australia) and read through echoes with California’s Imperial Valley, the project examines how spectral time—the co-presence and haunting of other temporalities—manifests in the material conditions of salt, soil, water, plants, and infrastructures. It asks how learning from geological, First Nations, colonial, and ecological pasts can orient responsibilities in unsettled futures. Treating the present as a crisis of time as much as a crisis of matter, the thesis critiques linear-progressive temporalities bound to Western modernity and extractive regimes. In response, spectral materialism is developed as both a conceptual framework and a critical creative methodology. Through alchemical media experiments with salt crystals, hypersaline soils, and halophytes, photography is reconfigured as a site-responsive, process-oriented practice. Salt is engaged as a material agent and ‘time-crystal’ whose phase shifts—dissolution, saturation, precipitation, crystallisation, evaporation—form a meta-chemistry that refracts deep-marine pasts, settler-colonial irrigation infrastructures, and contemporary dust into processual renderings of time. Methodologically, the project advances attunement as a mode of sensing and responsiveness to forces that are not always immediately perceptible yet are materially active. Field notes appear as para-writing, interrupting linear narration so that heterogeneous times co-present themselves within the text. The thesis is guided by First Nations temporalities—time as relational and in place—while remaining accountable to ethical limits and protocols. The contribution is twofold: a theoretical articulation of spectral materialism as a way to think time otherwise, and a set of site-responsive methods for engaging elemental media in saline environments. Together, they generate materially grounded accounts of spectral presences and open alternative pathways for knowing, sensing, and relating within land-time-scapes marked by enduring colonial and ecological afterlives amid planetary change.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND COMMERCIALIZATION OF COMPUTATIONAL METHODS TO ACCELERATE DERMATOLOGICAL DISCOVERY
authors: Jasson Makkar
abstract: The skin is the largest and outermost organ that surrounds the human body and provides a physical barrier that protects the more delicate internal tissues from the harsh surrounding environment. Over the course of evolution, specialized structures have also arisen in the skin, including sweat and sebaceous glands, nails and claws, and hair follicles. The hair follicle is a multi-lineage mini-organ that is a critical component in defining mammalian species. The gain of function derived from hair and fur benefited these species for millennia due to its insulative and protective properties, mechanosensing function, and ability to serve as camouflage. Current approaches to assess these fibers are generally non-quantitative or are low throughput due to technical limitations of ‘splitting hairs’. We developed a novel deep learning-based computer vision approach for the high throughput quantification of individual hair fibers at a high resolution. Our innovative computer vision tool can distinguish and extract overlapping fibers for quantification of multivariate features including length, width, and color to generate single-hair phenomes (shPhenome) of diverse conditions across the lifespan of mice. Using our tool, we explored the effects of hormone signaling, genetic modifications, and aging on hair follicle output. These analyses revealed novel hair phenotypes as a result of endocrinological, developmental, and aging-related alterations in the fur coats of mice. This tool was then adapted to capture more nuanced hair phenotypes, such as curvature, in a variety of mouse models harboring genetic perturbations. Commercialization of the deep hair phenomics technology presented a unique opportunity to pursue research translation, transforming fundamental biological research into marketable products. Much like the traditional academic route, the path to commercialization requires consistent and continuous iteration, testing of hypotheses, and allowing data to influence and lead subsequent actions. However, as opposed to the pursuit of knowledge, translating research into market-ready solutions requires a focus on consumer needs and the identification of market opportunities. Additionally, the shift in incentive structure requires commercial ventures to prioritize intellectual property protection, alter capital and resource allocation, and seek alternative fundraising sources. The entrepreneurial foundation built through this process culminated in the filing of a provisional patent and establishment of a startup company, kerat Inc. This journey illuminated the multifaceted challenges inherent in closing the gap between academic innovation and commercially viable goods, requiring simultaneous advancement of technical capabilities, adaptation to market dynamics, and fabrication of business infrastructure. Overall, the culmination of work presented in this dissertation sheds light on the importance of quantitatively assessing hair fiber properties to capture the biological phenomena that underlie this fundamental feature of mammalian skin. These findings also highlight the capabilities of this methodology for identifying perturbations in normal growth, potentially indicative of disease or dysfunction. Lastly, this showcased the potential of this technology’s commercial use cases in both the cosmetics and diagnostics industries.
